title: Who Gets to Connect the Dots?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino, a science teacher, describes the familiar gap between students who seem to follow a big-picture explanation of the circulatory system and the same students being unable to link the ideas weeks later. She asks who is doing the connecting, since a teacher who draws every arrow may be robbing students of the chance to make the links themselves. She does not conclude that teachers should stop explaining, because a clear explanation reduces incorrect connections, but argues that hearing an expert make a link is not the same as being able to retrieve and use it. Her approach is to decide in advance which links students must make, activate the prior knowledge needed, explain in manageable steps with students answering as she goes, and then fade guidance over later lessons. Fading is driven by what student responses reveal rather than a fixed timetable.
points: Decide beforehand which connections students must be able to explain, and pre-activate the knowledge those links depend on.
Model the linking thinking, but have students retrieve, consider and explain each step so they are not merely watching the teacher join dots.
Fade support for explaining whole concepts over time, for example by removing the word list in a later lesson and changing the question weeks afterwards.
Use student explanations diagnostically to see whether the gap is a missing fact, an imprecise explanation or a misconception, then adjust support.
quotes: A few students look at me as if something has clicked. That’s a good sign! This is the big picture I wanted them to see.
This is something I have always struggled with- my students seem to get something in lessons, but then they don’t do as well in assessments.
If I draw the whole picture and explain every link, have I helped students make meaning, or have I robbed them of an opportunity to make concrete links themselves?

But hearing a connection made by an expert is not the same as being able to retrieve and use it. We need to model the thinking, then give students opportunities to do more of that thinking themselves.
Just as we fade guidance with complex tasks, we need to consider how to fade our support on explaining whole concepts.

Fading guidance is not about removing support according to a fixed timetable. It is about using what students show us to decide where they are ready to think more independently and where they need more of our support.
I want to know not only whether they remember the facts, but whether they can still connect them when I am no longer drawing the arrows for them.
